title: Insurance Credentialing: Steps, Documents and Timeline
summary: Insurance credentialing for group practices: the 6 steps, a documents checklist, 90 to 180 day timelines, and how to estimate what a delay costs.
body_markdown:
Insurance credentialing is the payer's check that a clinician is licensed, trained and insured before it pays for their sessions. Until a payer approves a clinician and sets an effective date, that clinician cannot bill the payer as in-network.


For a group practice, credentialing decides when a new hire starts producing revenue. This guide covers the steps, the documents, realistic timelines, and how to work out what a delay costs you per clinician.

## What insurance credentialing is, and how contracting differs


Getting a clinician in network with a payer happens in two phases. Both have to finish before the first in-network claim.


- Credentialing: the payer verifies the clinician's license, education, work history, malpractice cover and sanctions record, then a committee approves or declines.
- Contracting: the payer offers a participation agreement with a fee schedule. You review the rates, sign, and the payer issues an effective date.
- Loading: after signing, the payer adds the clinician to its claims system. Claims sent before that date can deny even when the contract is signed.


Credentialing is per clinician and per payer. A new hire joining five panels runs five separate applications.


## How long insurance credentialing takes


Timelines vary by payer and state. One credentialing services firm,[The Credentialing Company](https://thecredentialing.com/blogs/what-is-insurance-credentialing) , puts them at:


Payer type Typical time to approval


Commercial plans (for example Aetna, Cigna, UnitedHealthcare) 60 to 120 days for a complete application


Medicare and Medicaid 90 to 150 days, depending on regional and state backlogs


Overall, per health plan 90 to 180 days


Application with an error Can move to the back of the queue and pass six months


Contracting and system loading can add weeks after approval. Plan from the effective date, never from the approval email.


## How to get credentialed with insurance companies: 6 steps


1. Choose the payers. List the plans your current patients use and the plans in your referral area. Each panel is a separate application, so start with the ones that matter most.
2. Build or update the CAQH profile. Most commercial payers pull clinician data from CAQH, and you authorize each payer to view it.
3. Submit each payer's application. Use the payer's own portal or form, and match every detail to the CAQH profile.
4. Follow up on a fixed schedule. Log the submission date and check status every two weeks until a decision arrives.
5. Review the contract and fee schedule. Check the rates for the codes you bill most before you sign.
6. Confirm the effective date in writing. Bill as in-network only from that date, and only once the payer has loaded the clinician.


## Insurance credentialing checklist: documents to collect before day one


Most delays start with a missing or mismatched document. Collect these before the application goes in.


Credentialing document checklist


- **License:** current state license, with expiry date and any supervision agreement for pre-licensed clinicians.
- **NPI:** individual NPI and taxonomy code, plus the group NPI if you bill as a group.
- **Tax ID:** the practice EIN and a completed W-9.
- **CAQH profile:** complete, attested, and authorized for each payer.
- **Malpractice cover:** certificate of insurance with limits and dates.
- **Education:** degrees, transcripts and board certifications where they apply.
- **Work history:** CV with month and year for every role, and a written note for any gap.
- **Practice details:** service locations, telehealth status and hours, matching across every form.


The name, address and tax details must match across the NPI record, CAQH, the W-9 and the application. A mismatch is one of the easiest ways to stall a file.


## What a credentialing delay costs a group practice


A clinician who joins before credentialing clears either sees fewer insured patients or sees them self-pay. The gap between hire date and first in-network claim has a cost you can estimate.


### How to calculate revenue exposure per new hire


1. Count the insured sessions the clinician would see per week once in network.
2. Multiply by your average allowed amount per session for that payer mix.
3. Multiply by the weeks between start date and effective date.


Here is an example with assumed numbers. Replace them with your own.


Input (example) Value


Insured sessions per week 20


Average allowed amount per session $100


Weeks waiting (about 90 days) 13


Sessions not billable in network 260


Revenue at risk for one hire $26,000


The same math runs again for every payer a clinician adds later, and for every hire after that.

## Keeping credentials active as the practice grows


Credentialing does not end at approval. CAQH profiles run on a[120-day attestation cycle](https://www.dataspring.com/clinicians) , and payers re-credential clinicians periodically. A lapsed profile can stop claims weeks later.


One tracker per clinician and payer keeps this visible. These columns cover what you need:


Clinician Payer Submitted Next follow-up Effective date CAQH attestation due


Clinician A Payer 1 date every 2 weeks date from the payer every 120 days


Clinician A Payer 2 date every 2 weeks pending same profile


Clinician B Payer 1 date every 2 weeks pending every 120 days


- Start applications 120 to 180 days before a clinician's first patient day, as The Credentialing Company advises.
- Give one person ownership of the tracker. Shared ownership is how follow-ups slip.
- Re-check the tracker before every new payer or new location.

## Streamline Your Practice


Insurance credentialing sets the date a new clinician can bill. Everything after that date is a billing workflow.[Book a demo](https://www.mdhub.ai/book-demo) to see how mdhub runs eligibility, claims and denials for behavioral health practices.


Can a clinician see insured patients before credentialing is approved?


They can see patients, but claims to that payer as an in-network provider will usually deny until the effective date. Some payers allow limited retroactive billing and many do not. Check each payer's written policy, and use self-pay with informed consent where the policy does not allow it.


How long does insurance credentialing take?


Plan for 90 to 180 days per health plan. Commercial plans often take 60 to 120 days for a complete application, and Medicare and Medicaid often take 90 to 150 days. Errors can push a file past six months.


Does adding a new payer mean starting credentialing again?


Yes. Each payer runs its own credentialing and contract. A new payer means a new application and a new timeline, even for a clinician in network elsewhere.


What is CAQH and why does it matter for credentialing?


CAQH, now DataSpring, is the shared profile most commercial payers read clinician data from. You authorize each payer to view it and re-attest every 120 days. A stale profile is a common reason applications stall.
